source.title: Emerging Cross-lingual Structure in Pretrained Language Models
source.authors: Shijie Wu; Alexis Conneau; Haoran Li; Luke Zettlemoyer; Veselin Stoyanov

record.tranche_reason: The study measures similarity between independently trained language models and tests whether a linear mapping aligns their representations, using cross-lingual alignment and CKA rather than the original sources’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on cross-lingual representation similarity, linear alignment, and transfer. Mentioned prior-work findings are not included as rows. The transfer task results are included only where they evaluate representations after alignment; training details and hyperparameter choices are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains monolingual BERTs independently, in different languages and from different seeds. It measures their representational similarity with CKA against a random-encoder baseline and tests whether an orthogonal linear map aligns them at the word, contextual-word and sentence levels. These results bear on V3, V4, V6 and V7 using methods different from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that parameter sharing, not shared vocabulary or domain, drives multilingual MLM transfer. They also conclude that independently trained monolingual BERTs in different languages can be aligned post hoc by an orthogonal map, suggesting universal latent symmetries. CKA shows early layers are more similar than late layers, and all effects are stronger for closely related languages.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines multilingual pretraining, post-hoc cross-lingual orthogonal alignment, and CKA similarity; it does not reproduce either named original source’s method.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity and alignment vary by layer and language pair. Early layers show higher CKA similarity; higher layers perform better for contextual word retrieval, while sentence retrieval is best in lower layers and downstream transfer peaks at middle layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In bilingual MLMs, cross-lingual transfer depends mainly on sharing top-layer parameters; anchor points, a shared softmax and domain similarity matter little (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared parameters, not shared vocabulary, drive cross-lingual representational alignment in jointly trained models.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Many plotted alignment results are figure-only in the provided text; no uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported similarity results. The study uses a fixed model size and does not test scale or capability trends.
record.rows_left_out: The bilingual MLM ablation results in Table 1 are not included: they measure downstream cross-lingual transfer under changes to shared vocabulary, domain, and parameter sharing, rather than directly measuring the claim versions’ representational similarity or alignment. Appendix Figure 8 compares additional bilingual-MLM alignment variants and is likewise outside the selected rows.

untested.parts: All of it: there is a single fixed model size and no scale or capability trend.
All of it: no vision models.
Shared individual features, subspaces or units; the only cross-seed evidence is one CKA comparison.
Stitching, relative representations, and unsupervised (unpaired) mapping.
All of it: no interpretable features or circuits.
Alternative similarity metrics, neighbour-count settings, and out-of-distribution inputs.
Plateau with scale; causal isolation of shared data or objective for the monolingual models.

missing.what: CKA is highly correlated with sentence-level alignment performance (Pearson >0.9 for all four pairs). This shows two measures agreeing, which bears against metric dependence.
Per-layer CKA numbers in Figure 7 are tabulated, e.g. en-en′ monolingual L7 0.24 vs random 0.32 and L1 0.77 vs 0.60. Rows r1 and r7 treat these as averages only or as figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The random-encoder CKA baseline is high (0.41–0.50), so monolingual similarity gains are modest. The cross-seed comparison (en-en′) uses back-translated paraphrase inputs, not identical sentences. Many alignment values are readable only from figures.

versions.untested_parts: No model size or capability sweep, and no test of convergence as scale or performance increases.
No vision-language models or paired images and captions.
The same-language, different-seed comparison uses CKA similarity; the paper does not identify recurring interpretable features, shared subspaces, or individual units.
Tests orthogonal linear mapping, not stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified or compared.
The paper varies representation layer and language pair, but does not systematically compare similarity metrics, metric settings such as neighbour count, or out-of-distribution inputs.
The paper compares monolingual and bilingual representations, but does not isolate shared training data or objectives as causal explanations, nor test a scale-related plateau.

rows.subject: monolingual BERT (English–English′)
rows.operation_detail: Average CKA similarity across layers L0–L8 for English models trained with different random seeds
rows.note: The English′ monolingual model was trained on the same data as English with a different random seed. The paper also reports a bilingual English–English′ model at 0.68.
rows.check: Averaged CKA 0.59 vs random 0.50. Per layer (Fig 7) it is 0.77 vs 0.52 at L1 but 0.24 vs 0.32 at L7, i.e. below random. Inputs also differ: en′ is a back-translated paraphrase, not identical sentences. Not linked to V6, since varying language pair is not a metric or input-choice manipulation.

relationships.condition: Contextual word retrieval, NER and parsing transfer for other pairs, and sentence retrieval
relationships.reason: Retrieval is below fastText (r9). Transfer is below jointly trained biMLM, with a larger gap for NER (r11–r15). Sentence retrieval is good but below LASER (r16–r19). All are layer-dependent.
relationships.display_finding: Word retrieval trailed fastText, NER and parsing transfer trailed jointly trained biMLM especially for NER, and sentence retrieval trailed LASER, with all results depending on layer choice.

relationships.reason: CKA and sentence retrieval peak at low layers, word retrieval at high layers, and transfer at middle layers. CKA reaches or falls below random at L7 (r7, r9, r10, r16–r19). Note the authors report CKA correlates with sentence retrieval at r>0.9.
relationships.display_finding: CKA and sentence retrieval peaked in lower layers, word retrieval in higher layers, and transfer in middle layers; CKA reached or fell below random at layer 7, despite correlating with sentence retrieval at r>0.9.
